title: A Spark as Big as the Sky

pages.text: In the dry days of harmattan, pull a nylon shirt over your head in a dark room. It crackles, and you may see tiny blue sparks. Run a plastic comb through dry hair, hold it over scraps of paper, and the scraps jump up to meet it. Nothing is plugged in. There is no battery. Yet electricity is at work. This kind is called static electricity, because the electric charge builds up and stays in one place until it suddenly escapes. That little spark on your shirt has a giant relative. You know it as lightning.

pages.text: Everything is made of atoms, and atoms contain tiny particles called electrons, which carry a negative charge. Usually an object has no overall charge. When two different materials rub together, electrons can be scraped from one onto the other. The one that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The one that loses them becomes positively charged. Then a simple rule takes over: opposite charges attract, and like charges repel. That is why the comb pulls on the paper. It is also why two balloons rubbed on the same cloth push each other apart.

pages.alt: Two balloons hanging on threads and pushing apart, beside a comb and a scrap of paper pulling together.

pages.text: Inside a tall storm cloud, strong winds toss ice crystals and small hailstones against each other millions of times a second. Each collision moves a little charge. Before long, the bottom of the cloud holds a huge negative charge. It repels electrons in the ground below, leaving the surface positive. Air is normally an insulator, but when the voltage grows large enough, the air breaks down and a giant spark leaps across. For an instant the air in its path is heated to about 30,000 °C, five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air expands with a bang. That is thunder.

pages.text: In 1752, the American scientist Benjamin Franklin suspected that lightning was the same thing as the sparks in his laboratory. The story goes that he flew a kite towards a storm cloud with a metal key tied to the string. Charge ran down the wet string, and a spark jumped from the key to his knuckle. He was right, and he was lucky: others who tried similar experiments were killed. His idea led to the lightning conductor, a metal rod on top of a building joined by a thick wire to the ground. It gives lightning a safe path, away from the building.

pages.text: How big is the voltage in a storm cloud? Flying instruments into one is dangerous, so scientists at Ooty in southern India found a safer way. Their detectors count muons, tiny particles that rain down on Earth from space all the time. During a great storm in December 2014, the number of muons arriving changed, because the cloud’s electric field had changed their energy as they passed through. From this, the team worked out the voltage inside the cloud: about 1.3 billion volts. They measured the storm without touching or disturbing it.

From this, the team worked out the voltage inside the cloud: about 1.3 billion volts.
They measured the storm without touching or disturbing it.
pages.alt: A wide field of flat particle detectors on a hilltop under a towering storm cloud.

pages.text: Every rainy season, lightning kills people in Ghana, often on farms, on football pitches, and under trees. Follow these rules. When you hear thunder, go indoors or into a vehicle with a metal roof, and stay there until 30 minutes after the last thunder. Never shelter under a lone tree, because lightning tends to strike the tallest thing around. Leave open fields, hilltops, rivers, and the sea. Indoors, keep away from taps and from anything plugged into a socket. If a person is struck, it is safe to touch them. Call for help and start first aid.

activities.question: What happens when two different materials are rubbed together?
options: Electrons can move from one material to the other

activities.question: What causes thunder?
options: Air heated by the lightning expanding suddenly

activities.question: Why was the method used at Ooty better than flying a kite into a storm?
options: It was safer and did not disturb the storm being studied
It was cheaper than a kite

activities.question: Apply it: You are playing football on an open pitch when you hear thunder. A large mango tree stands nearby. What should you do?
options: Leave the pitch and go into a building, not under the tree
Lie flat in the middle of the pitch and keep playing later

activities.prompt: Put the steps that lead to a flash of lightning in order.
items: Ice crystals and hailstones collide inside the cloud
A large negative charge gathers at the bottom of the cloud
The ground below becomes positively charged
The air breaks down and a giant spark jumps
Heated air expands and makes thunder

glossary.definition: Static electricity: electric charge that builds up in one place until it suddenly escapes.
A property of matter that can be positive or negative.
